1

Composite Response

Prompt 1: Can someone committed to the absence of objective free will also claim there is subjective free will?

Subjective agency can survive even if objective free will does not

Yes. Objective free will and subjective free will answer different questions. Objective free will asks whether a choice could break free from the total causal story of the world. Subjective free will asks what choosing feels like from the inside and what practical distinctions remain visible within deliberation.

A determinist can therefore deny contra-causal freedom while still affirming that persons compare options, imagine consequences, hesitate, commit, regret, and revise. None of that requires a metaphysical gap in causation. It only requires that complex organisms model futures and act through those models.

The confusion begins when first-person vocabulary is treated as if it were already a metaphysical theory. Saying “I chose” can simply mean that the action passed through my values, reasons, memory, and forecasting capacities rather than through seizure, compulsion, or external override.

  1. Objective level: Could the agent have done otherwise in the exact same total state of the universe?
  2. Subjective level: Did the agent deliberate, evaluate reasons, and experience authorship from the inside?
  3. Practical payoff: The distinction protects ordinary agency talk without pretending it resolves the metaphysical dispute.

What to notice

  • Keep first-person experience and public explanation in view without letting either do all the work.
  • Do not let a phenomenological description quietly turn into a metaphysical conclusion.
2

Composite Response

Prompt 2: So, the determinist need not give up terms that reflect personal agency such as “choose” and “decide” if they are willing to make clear in relevant contexts that they are referring to subjective free will, right?

Determinists can keep agency language if they state its level clearly

Right. A determinist does not need to purge the language of choice any more than a biologist needs to stop using the word “heart” after learning about cells. In ordinary life, “choose” usually marks a psychologically mediated action: the person considered options, responded to reasons, and acted through their own cognitive machinery.

That remains compatible with determinism. What the determinist should avoid is the stronger claim that the person stood outside causation and selected among genuinely open alternatives in an identical universe-state. That is where the vocabulary outruns the theory.

This matters in law, therapy, education, and everyday accountability. We constantly need to distinguish impulsive action from reflective action, manipulation from consent, and compulsion from normal deliberation. Agency terms remain useful because those differences are real even if libertarian freedom is not.

  1. Keep the language: “Choose,” “decide,” and “intend” still track meaningful differences in human behavior.
  2. State the level: They refer to deliberative processes within a causal system, not to magical exemption from it.
  3. Avoid overreach: Agency language misleads only when it is recruited as evidence for objective free will.

What to notice

  • Keep first-person experience and public explanation in view without letting either do all the work.
  • Agency language can remain practical and discriminating without becoming metaphysically inflated.
3

Composite Response

Prompt 3: Given this conclusion, is there any field other than metaphysics in which a strong determinist stance from a determinist would be productive or required?

Where strong determinism helps outside metaphysics

A strong determinist stance is productive wherever the task is to explain, predict, or redesign behavior rather than preserve an intuitive picture of desert. Neuroscience and psychology are the clearest cases, because those fields already assume that thought and action arise from causes that can be studied.

Criminal justice is another serious arena. Determinism does not automatically abolish restraint, deterrence, or public safety, but it does weaken the fantasy that punishment is metaphysically deserved in some absolute sense. That pressure pushes the conversation toward rehabilitation, prevention, and redesign of upstream social conditions.

Education, public policy, and AI also benefit from causal thinking. Teachers, legislators, and system designers all work by altering incentives, environments, and capacities. The main caution is not to let determinism flatten moral language so much that differences between coercion, negligence, competence, and impairment disappear.

  1. Neuroscience and psychology: determinism is almost built into the search for causes.
  2. Criminal justice: it redirects attention from metaphysical blame to prevention and rehabilitation.
  3. Education and policy: it encourages redesign of conditions rather than moralizing over outcomes alone.
  4. AI and decision theory: it clarifies that behavior can be shaped through architecture, incentives, and feedback loops.

What to notice

  • Determinism is most useful where causal explanation improves intervention.
  • The danger is not determinism itself, but letting it erase distinctions needed for humane judgment.
4

Composite Response

Prompt 4: Create a dialogue between two determinists. The first is a cognitive scientist who feels it is quite reasonable to punish criminals for their crimes for at least the sake of deterrence, and the second is a criminal justice advocate who feels it is wrong to punish criminals for following an unavoidable causal path to the crime.

A dialogue that tests what Subjective/Objective Free Will can explain

The real pressure here is whether rejecting objective free will also rules out punishment. It does not. The harder question is what justifies punishment once desert is no longer doing the deepest work.

The reader should leave with a narrower disagreement, a clearer picture of the main pressure point, and a better sense of what evidence or distinction would matter next.

Cognitive Scientist (CS) If behavior is causally produced, that does not make deterrence irrational. Penalties can still become part of the environment that lowers future harm.

Criminal Justice Advocate (CJA) I grant that consequences influence behavior. My objection is to punitive theater that treats offenders as metaphysically deserving suffering rather than as dangerous, damaged, or dysregulated people.

CS Then maybe the word “punishment” is doing too much work. We still need incapacitation, warning signals, and predictable costs for serious harms.

CJA Yes, but those tools should be justified forward-lookingly: protecting others, changing future behavior, and repairing damage when possible. Retribution is the part determinism puts under strain.

CS I can accept that. A prison sentence might still be warranted, but its rationale should be public safety and deterrence, not cosmic payback.

CJA Exactly. Determinism does not remove consequences; it changes how we talk about them. The system should ask what reduces future violence with the least gratuitous cruelty.

CS Then the dispute is narrower than it first looked. We both accept causal management. We disagree about how much suffering the state may impose once retribution is off the table.

CJA Right. Determinism should make a justice system humbler, more preventive, and less addicted to the rhetoric of blame.

What to notice

  • The debate is not consequences versus no consequences.
  • The sharper issue is retribution versus forward-looking social protection.
